sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to Simulator 12.7A: Small-File Compaction and Query Latency Studio! Adjust the file count and average micro-file size to analyze HTTP TLS overhead, and execute bin-packing compaction to evaluate scan speedups.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Kaito, let us investigate Simulator 12.7A. Notice how reading thousands of tiny 128-kilobyte files wastes over ninety percent of execution time on HTTP handshakes! Watch the latency collapse when we compact them into optimal 256-megabyte segments!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 12.7.1: Small-File Latency Degradation and Compaction Speedup. Calculate the baseline scan latency across 10,000 micro-files and the speedup achieved after compacting into 256-megabyte target segments.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Checkpoint 12.7.1 time! With 10,000 files averaging 200 kilobytes over a 1 gigabyte per second network, what is our total uncompacted scan time, and how much faster is it after bin-packing compaction?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Outstanding! With a 20-millisecond HTTP penalty per file, 10,000 requests consume 200 seconds of protocol overhead plus 2 seconds of transfer, totaling 202 seconds. Compacting into 8 target files slashes HTTP overhead to 0.16 seconds, delivering a massive 14.8 times speedup!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Incorrect. 10,000 files at 20 milliseconds each incur 200 seconds of HTTP handshake overhead, plus 2 seconds of network transfer. Compacting into 8 files reduces HTTP latency to 0.16 seconds plus 2 seconds of transfer, yielding a 14.8 times speedup.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to Simulator 12.7B: Compliance Erasure and Deletion Vector Studio! Trigger GDPR Article 17 deletion requests and compare naive Copy-on-Write full file rewrites against Roaring Bitmap deletion vectors.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Kaito, let us explore Simulator 12.7B! Look at the write amplification gauge when we delete a single patient record under Copy-on-Write: rewriting a 256-megabyte file to erase 1 kilobyte causes 262,000 times write amplification! Notice how deletion vectors eliminate this entirely!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 12.7.2: Object Storage API Cost Explosion Model. Determine the critical query threshold Q star where S3 GET request fees surpass the entire monthly physical storage bill for an uncompacted dataset.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Checkpoint 12.7.2! If our dataset has 500,000 small files taking only 50 gigabytes of storage, at what number of table scans do API request charges exceed the storage cost?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Brilliant! Fifty gigabytes costs only 1 dollar and 15 cents monthly in storage. But 500,000 files cost 20 cents per full scan in S3 GET requests. Thus, at just 6 table scans per month, API request fees exceed the entire physical storage cost!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Incorrect. Physical storage costs 50 gigabytes times 2.3 cents equals 1 dollar and 15 cents. Each scan of 500,000 files at 0.40 dollars per million requests costs 20 cents. Dividing 1.15 by 0.20 yields approximately 5.75, so at 6 queries, API fees exceed storage.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 12.7.3: Compliance Write Amplification Elimination. Calculate the exact write amplification factor of Copy-on-Write rewrites versus Roaring Bitmap deletion vectors when purging a 1-kilobyte record from a 256-megabyte Parquet file.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Checkpoint 12.7.3! Comparing traditional file rewrites to deletion vector bitmaps, what is the exact write amplification difference when fulfilling a GDPR deletion request?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Outstanding! Rewriting 256 megabytes to erase 1 kilobyte incurs a write amplification factor of 262,144 times. In contrast, appending a 4-byte bitmap tombstone incurs an amplification of just 0.0039 times, representing a 99.999 percent reduction in I/O bandwidth!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Incorrect. 256 megabytes divided by 1 kilobyte is 262,144 times write amplification. A 4-byte bitmap row index divided by 1,024 bytes is 0.0039 times, slashing write amplification by over 99.999 percent.
